questions.question: What is RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)?
scoring_points: Describes indexing path: parse, chunk, embed, store vectors with metadata
Describes query path: embed query, retrieve top-k, re-rank, generate grounded answer
Notes that RAG failures usually start at retrieval, not generation

questions.question: Where does RAG usually fail first?
scoring_points: Identifies retrieval as the primary failure point, not the generator
Mentions wrong chunk or missing chunk as common retrieval failures
Suggests evaluating retrieval and generation separately

questions.question: How should a RAG system decide to say 'I don't know'?
scoring_points: Combines signals: low retrieval scores below a calibrated threshold
Uses a verifier step that checks the draft answer against sources
Evaluates refusal precision as well as answer accuracy

questions.question: Explain the transformer architecture
scoring_points: Describes multi-head self-attention letting every token mix information from others
Mentions residual connections, layer normalization, and feed-forward network per block
Notes O(n²) cost in sequence length and that modern LLMs are decoder-only

questions.question: Why do most LLMs use decoder-only instead of encoder-decoder?
scoring_points: One stack, one objective, scales simply
Handles generation natively without cross-attention complexity
Training and serving infrastructure is simpler to optimize

questions.question: Why divide by sqrt(d_k) in attention?
scoring_points: Without it, dot products grow with dimension
Softmax saturates with large inputs, producing near-one-hot distributions
Gradients vanish through the saturated softmax

questions.question: What is an AI agent, and how is it different from a chain?
scoring_points: Chain is a fixed sequence; agent is a loop where model chooses next action
Mentions ReAct pattern: reasoning step, tool call, observation
Notes agents handle open-ended tasks but are less predictable

questions.question: Explain the ReAct pattern.
scoring_points: Reason + Act: model alternates reasoning, tool call, and observation
Continues until it can answer the original question
Production needs step limits, structured tool calls, and error handling

questions.question: Single agent vs multi-agent systems: when is multi-agent worth it?
scoring_points: Start with single agent unless parallel work or permission separation needed
Multi-agent adds cost: token use grows, hand-offs lose context, failures harder to locate
Prototype both and switch only when quality or speed clearly improves

questions.question: RAG vs fine-tuning: when should you use each?
scoring_points: RAG for private or changing knowledge; fine-tuning for consistent format or behavior
They are not exclusive: fine-tuned model plus RAG is common
Knowledge goes in retrieval; behavior goes in the weights

questions.question: What is model distillation and when would you use it?
scoring_points: Transfers behavior from a large teacher to a smaller student via fine-tuning on teacher outputs
Use when a strong model handles a well-defined task but serving cost is too high
Validate on held-out set against ground truth, not just teacher agreement

questions.question: Fine-tuning vs in-context learning: what is the difference?
scoring_points: In-context learning puts examples in the prompt and changes no weights
Fine-tuning changes weights with training examples and needs data, eval, redeployment
Start with prompting; fine-tune only when prompting cannot hold the behavior

questions.question: How do you reduce LLM latency?
scoring_points: Split latency into TTFT (prefill) and generation (decode), trace to find dominant part
Streaming, shorter outputs, prefix caching, small routing models, parallel tool calls
Track p50 and p95 separately because tail latency is what users complain about

questions.question: What is LLM quantization and why does it matter?
scoring_points: Fewer bits per weight means smaller model, fits on smaller GPU
Decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, so fewer bytes means more tokens per second
Re-run task evals after quantizing because degradation is uneven across tasks

questions.question: What is the KV cache and why does it matter for inference?
scoring_points: Keys and values of earlier tokens are stored and reused; each new token computes only its own
Memory grows with sequence length and often limits batch size more than weights
Mitigations: grouped-query attention, KV quantization, paged allocation (PagedAttention)

questions.question: What do temperature and top-p do in an LLM?
scoring_points: Temperature rescales logits: near zero is focused, higher is more varied
Top-p trims the distribution to smallest set of tokens covering p probability
Set by task: low for extraction/code, higher for creative; adjust one, not both

questions.question: What is the difference between an embedding model and a generative model?
scoring_points: Embedding model outputs a fixed-length vector for comparison; generative model produces tokens
Embeddings are cheap enough for millions of documents; generative models cost more per call
In RAG: embed chunks once, embed query at request time, then pay for generation

questions.question: What is hybrid search and when should you use it?
scoring_points: Runs lexical (BM25) and dense (embedding) retrieval over same corpus
Uses rank fusion (e.g., reciprocal rank fusion) to combine results
Use when queries contain identifiers, error codes, or jargon that embeddings blur

questions.question: HNSW vs IVF: how do vector indexes trade off recall, speed and memory?
scoring_points: HNSW: multi-layer graph, excellent recall and latency, but high memory from graph links
IVF: cluster-based, lower memory especially with PQ, but recall drops if nprobe is low
Measure recall@10 against exact search on sample queries before choosing parameters

questions.question: How do you choose a chunking strategy for RAG?
scoring_points: Follow document structure (headings, paragraphs, code blocks) rather than fixed character counts
Small chunks give sharper embeddings; large chunks give more context; small-to-parent is a compromise
Compare strategies on real questions with known answer passages, not by intuition

questions.question: What is prompt injection and how do you defend against it?
scoring_points: Untrusted text overrides developer intent; indirect injection through retrieved content is harder
No prompt fully prevents it because instructions and data share one channel
Defend in layers: least-privilege tools, human confirmation, input/output filtering, audit logs

questions.question: Why do LLMs hallucinate, and how do you reduce it?
scoring_points: Model is trained to produce plausible continuations, not verify facts
Ground answers in retrieved sources, allow 'I don't know', constrain with schemas
Measure by breaking answers into claims and checking each against sources

questions.question: What is function calling (tool calling) in LLMs?
scoring_points: Model returns structured call (name + arguments) instead of text; your code executes it
Quality depends on tool design: small set, non-overlapping, clear descriptions, enums
Validate arguments, check permissions, require confirmation for side-effecting actions

questions.question: What is chain-of-thought prompting and when does it help?
scoring_points: Getting the model to write intermediate reasoning before the answer
Helps most on multi-step tasks; adds little to simple classification or fact lookup
Costs output tokens and latency; treat reasoning as debugging aid, not proof

questions.question: What is tokenization in LLMs and why does it matter?
scoring_points: Turns text into integer IDs using subword tokenizers like BPE
Everything is metered in tokens: price, latency, context window
Token efficiency differs by language; explains failures like letter counting
